items.stem: State what is meant by the term "two-way table".
items.answer: A table of frequencies classified by two categorical variables, used to find joint and conditional probabilities

items.stem: A test for a condition affecting 1% of people is 99% accurate for those who have it and gives false positives 5% of the time. Explain why a positive result is far from certain to mean the condition is present.
items.answer: P(condition | +) ≈ 0.167
items.markingKey: in 100 000 people about 990 true positives (R1) versus about 4950 false positives (R1); so P ≈ 0.167 (A1).

items.stem: Tariq says that events A and B with P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.2 and P(A ∩ B) = 0 are independent because "they don't affect each other". Explain why this is wrong.
items.answer: they are mutually exclusive, hence dependent
items.markingKey: independence requires P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.1 (R1); here P(A ∩ B) = 0 ≠ 0.1 (A1); knowing A occurred means B cannot occur, so they are dependent (R1).

items.stem: A fair coin shows heads 6 times in a row. Mei says the next toss is more likely to be tails. Explain whether this is correct.
items.answer: incorrect: P(tails) = 1/2
items.markingKey: tosses are independent (R1); the coin has no memory, so previous results do not affect the next (R1); P(tails) = 1/2 (A1).

items.stem: P(A) = 0.6 and P(B) = 0.7. Explain why A and B cannot be mutually exclusive, and find the least possible value of P(A ∩ B).
items.markingKey: if mutually exclusive, P(A ∪ B) = 1.3 > 1, impossible (R1); P(A ∩ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∪ B) ≥ 1.3 − 1 (M1); 0.3 (A1).

items.stem: A student claims: "If P(positive | disease) = 0.99, then P(disease | positive) = 0.99." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: These are different; P(disease | positive) also depends on how common the disease is and the false-positive rate.
items.markingKey: These are different; P(disease | positive) also depends on how common the disease is and the false-positive rate. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: P(A ∩ B) = 0.2, P(A) = 0.25 and P(B) = 0.8. Leila says P(A | B) = P(B | A). Explain why this is false and find both values.
items.markingKey: both use P(A ∩ B) but divide by different probabilities (R1); P(A | B) = 0.2/0.8 = 0.25 (A1); P(B | A) = 0.2/0.25 = 0.8 (A1).

items.stem: Explain the difference between independent and mutually exclusive events.
items.answer: Independent events do not affect each other's probabilities (P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)); mutually exclusive events cannot occur together (P(A ∩ B) = 0).
